title: Per-Client Rate Limiter
summary: Decide per client whether each request may proceed under fixed-window or token-bucket policies, with exact limits under heavy concurrent load and accurate retry-after hints.
statement:
Your company's public API is being hammered by a few heavy clients, starving everyone else. Before a request reaches business logic, it must pass an in-process rate limiter that decides — per client — whether to let it through.

**Policies**
Two kinds of policy are needed:
- **Fixed window** — at most L requests per window of W milliseconds. Windows are aligned to multiples of W since the epoch (with W = 60,000, windows start at :00 of each minute), and the count starts again in each new window.
- **Token bucket** — a bucket holds at most C tokens and starts full. Tokens are added continuously at R tokens per P milliseconds — fractions accumulate — but never beyond C. A request needs whole tokens.

Operators define named policies (for example "free": fixed window, 100 per minute; "pro": token bucket, capacity 50, refilling 10 per second) and assign clients to them. Clients without an assignment use a default policy. Moving a client to another policy takes effect from its next request, starting with fresh state under the new policy.

**Decisions**
- For each request the limiter receives a client id and an optional cost — the number of permits the request needs, 1 by default, never more than the policy's limit or capacity.
- It answers allowed or denied. An allowed request consumes its cost; a denied request consumes nothing.
- An allowed answer includes how many permits the client has left (requests left in the window, or whole tokens left in the bucket).
- A denied answer says how long the client should wait before the same request could be allowed: until the next window starts, or until enough tokens will have accumulated.
- Clients never affect each other's limits.

**Concurrency**
The limiter is called by every request-handling thread at once, often for the same hot client. Limits must hold exactly under that load — a client limited to 100 per window never gets 101 requests through — and calls for different clients should not queue behind one another.

The current time must come from a source tests can control. Further algorithms (for example a sliding window) are already on the roadmap.

requirements.text: Define named policies — fixed window (L ≥ 1, W ≥ 1 ms) or token bucket (C ≥ 1, R ≥ 1 tokens per P ≥ 1 ms) — designate a default policy, and assign clients to policies. Invalid parameters and unknown policy names are rejected.

Decide a request for a client: allowed or denied. Allowed answers consume the cost and report permits left; denied answers consume nothing and report the wait in milliseconds before the same request could be allowed. One client's requests never change another client's decisions.

Fixed window: windows are [k × W, (k + 1) × W); at most L permits are allowed per client per window; a request at the exact window start belongs to the new window; a denial waits until the next window starts.

Token bucket: starts full at C tokens, refills continuously at R per P ms without losing fractional tokens and never exceeds C; a request is allowed only if at least cost whole tokens are available; a denial waits until enough tokens will have accumulated (rounded up to the next millisecond).
Decisions are safe under concurrent calls for the same and different clients, with the guarantees given in the concurrency notes.
Requests may carry a cost from 1 up to the policy's L or C; a cost outside that range is rejected as invalid (an error, not a denial) and consumes nothing.
Reassigning a client to another policy takes effect from the client's next request with fresh state under the new policy.

constraints: Java 17 or later using only the standard library (java.util.concurrent is allowed); JUnit 5 may be used for tests.
Single JVM process with all state in memory; no external store or network.
Time is in milliseconds from a controllable source and never goes backwards.
Up to 100,000 active clients; each decision should take O(1) time.
Refilling 3 tokens per 1,000 ms must yield exactly 3 tokens after 1,000 ms, however many requests arrived in between.
assumptions: Client ids are non-empty strings supplied by a trusted caller.
Policies are defined before traffic starts; client assignments may change at any time.
Memory for idle clients is not a concern for this exercise.

examples.title: Fixed window
examples.scenario: Policy: fixed window, L = 3, W = 1,000 ms. Client c1 sends requests at t = 950, 960, 970, 980, 1,000, 1,001, 1,002 and 1,003 ms.
examples.expected: 950, 960 and 970 are allowed (2, 1, 0 left). 980 is denied with a wait of 20 ms. 1,000, 1,001 and 1,002 are allowed — a new window [1,000, 2,000) has started. 1,003 is denied with a wait of 997 ms. Six requests passed between t = 950 and t = 1,002, which is expected for fixed windows.

examples.title: Token bucket
examples.scenario: Policy: token bucket, C = 5, refilling 1 token per 200 ms. Client c2 sends 6 requests at t = 0, one at t = 100, one at t = 200, then 5 at t = 1,000.
examples.expected: At t = 0 the first 5 are allowed and the 6th is denied with a wait of 200 ms. At t = 100 the request is denied (0.5 tokens) with a wait of 100 ms. At t = 200 it is allowed (1 token had accrued, 0 left). At t = 1,000 the bucket holds 4 tokens: 4 requests are allowed and the 5th is denied with a wait of 200 ms.

examples.title: Requests with a cost
examples.scenario: Token bucket, C = 10, refilling 10 tokens per 1,000 ms. At t = 0 client c3 sends cost 7, then cost 5; at t = 200 cost 5; then cost 11.
examples.expected: Cost 7 is allowed (3 left). Cost 5 is denied with a wait of 200 ms. At t = 200 the bucket holds 5, so cost 5 is allowed (0 left). Cost 11 is rejected as invalid because it exceeds the capacity.

examples.title: Hot client under contention
examples.scenario: Fixed window, L = 100, W = 60,000 ms, time frozen at t = 5,000. 32 threads together send 1,000 requests for client "hot" while another thread sends 50 for client "calm".
examples.expected: Exactly 100 "hot" requests are allowed and 900 denied; all 50 "calm" requests are allowed.

edgeCases: A request exactly at a window boundary belongs to the new window.
A token bucket idle for an hour holds exactly C tokens, not more.
Fractional refill: with 3 tokens per 1,000 ms, after 500 ms there are 1.5 tokens, so one request is allowed and 0.5 tokens remain.
A cost of 0, a negative cost, or a cost above the limit/capacity is an invalid request, not a denial.
A client with no assignment uses the default policy.
A client is reassigned in the middle of a window: its next request starts fresh under the new policy.
Many requests share the same millisecond.
outOfScope: Rate limiting shared across processes or machines.
HTTP integration such as status codes and headers.
Loading policies from files or remote configuration.

concurrency.notes: Must be thread-safe: decisions for the same and different clients, policy assignment and reads may all run concurrently. Guarantees: (1) for a fixed-window client, allowed permits in one window never exceed L, and N concurrent unit-cost requests in a fresh window get exactly min(L, N) allowed; (2) for a token-bucket client, allowed cost over any interval never exceeds C plus the tokens refilled in that interval; (3) a denied request consumes nothing, and permits are never consumed twice or lost under contention; (4) a request racing with a reassignment is decided entirely under either the old or the new policy. Should: requests for different clients do not all serialise on one shared bottleneck.

acceptanceCriteria.text: With a controlled clock, the fixed-window example produces exactly the stated allow/deny decisions, permits left and waits (20 ms, 997 ms).
The token-bucket example produces exactly the stated decisions and waits (200 ms, 100 ms, 200 ms), and an idle bucket never exceeds its capacity.
Costs are honoured as in the cost example; an out-of-range cost is an error that consumes nothing.
The contention example passes repeatedly: exactly 100 allowed for "hot" and all 50 allowed for "calm".
Unassigned clients use the default policy, invalid policy parameters are rejected, and reassignment starts the client fresh under the new policy.

stretchGoals.text: Add a sliding-window policy that never allows more than L permits in any W-millisecond span.
Discard state for clients idle longer than 10 minutes without changing any decision the limiter would make.
Add a global limit shared by all clients that must also allow a request, in addition to the client’s own policy.

rubricGuidance.correctness: FR-2 to FR-4 carry the weight: window alignment and reset, continuous refill without drift, exact wait values and denied requests consuming nothing. The worked numbers (waits of 20/997 ms and 200/100/200 ms) should be reproduced exactly.
rubricGuidance.modeling: Look for a clear split between policy definitions (parameters), per-client state, client-to-policy assignment and the decision result. The two algorithms should sit side by side without a large type-switch threaded through the decision path.
rubricGuidance.principles: Per-client state should change only inside the decision operation, keeping check-and-consume atomic. Concurrency is required: check-then-act races between reading and consuming permits, or lost updates when creating per-client state, are serious defects whatever mechanism is used.
rubricGuidance.extensibility: The statement anticipates further algorithms (sliding window) and runtime reassignment. Adding an algorithm should not change client lookup or the concurrency handling. Do not reward speculative layers beyond that seam.
rubricGuidance.readability: Time arithmetic (window start, refill amount, wait) should live in small, named computations instead of being repeated inline.
rubricGuidance.edge_cases: Check boundary instants, invalid costs vs denials, refill capped at capacity, fractional refill, unknown clients and reassignment mid-window.
rubricGuidance.tests: Expect deterministic tests with a controllable clock for both algorithms plus a concurrent test asserting the exact allowed count for a hot client while another client is unaffected.
